content: Conventional treatments for primary dysmenorrhoea have a failure rate of 20% to 25%. Additionally, these treatments may be contraindicated or poorly tolerated by some women. Chinese herbal medicine has been proposed as a potential alternative therapy for this condition. The objective of this study was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of Chinese herbal medicine for primary dysmenorrhoea in comparison to placebo, no treatment, and other treatment modalities. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Menstrual Disorders and Subfertility Group Trials Register, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, AMED, CENTRAL, CNKI, TCMDS, and CBM, covering studies published up to January 2007. Citation lists of included trials were also reviewed. The inclusion criteria for the review were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared Chinese herbal medicine with placebo, no treatment, conventional therapy, heat compression, other types of Chinese herbal medicine, acupuncture, or massage. Trials were excluded if participants had identifiable pelvic pathology or dysmenorrhoea caused by intrauterine contraceptive devices. Data collection and analysis were conducted independently by two reviewers. Quality assessment, data extraction, and translation were performed, and study authors were contacted for additional information when necessary. Meta-analyses were conducted using Peto odds ratios or relative risk (RR) for dichotomous data and weighted mean difference for continuous data, employing a fixed-effect statistical model when appropriate. If meta-analysis was not feasible, descriptive data from the trials were presented. The review included 39 randomized controlled trials involving a total of 3,475 women. Many of these trials were small in sample size and of poor methodological quality. Results comparing Chinese herbal medicine to placebo were inconclusive due to insufficient data for meta-analysis (3 RCTs). However, when compared to pharmaceutical drugs, Chinese herbal medicine demonstrated significant improvements in pain relief (14 RCTs; RR 1.99, 95% CI 1.52 to 2.60), overall symptoms (6 RCTs; RR 2.17, 95% CI 1.73 to 2.73), and reduced use of additional medication (2 RCTs; RR 1.58, 95% CI 1.30 to 1.93). Self-designed Chinese herbal formulae showed significant benefits in pain relief (18 RCTs; RR 2.06, 95% CI 1.80 to 2.36), overall symptoms (14 RCTs; RR 1.99, 95% CI 1.65 to 2.40), and reduced use of additional medication (5 RCTs; RR 1.58, 95% CI 1.34 to 1.87) after up to three months of follow-up, compared to commonly used Chinese herbal health products. Furthermore, Chinese herbal medicine provided better pain relief than acupuncture (2 RCTs; RR 1.75, 95% CI 1.09 to 2.82) and heat compression (1 RCT; RR 2.08, 95% CI 2.06 to 499.18). The authors concluded that there is promising evidence supporting the use of Chinese herbal medicine for primary dysmenorrhoea. However, the findings are limited by the poor methodological quality of the included trials.
